)​

​
Let's start with our newsletter,

Last year, one of my Accelerator students (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/r8ulr2p0neaoh3486e6c2hdnlgw33t7h365er/n2hohvhvm0x7eof6/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
)​ sent me a message in January:

“I think I messed up. I’ve applied to 150 roles. Two interviews.
Both rejected. I don’t know if I’m built for this.”

He had:

* CMU admit
* Intel on his resume
* AI background
* Strong academics

And still… zero traction.

Let me tell you what actually changed his trajectory. A system
shift.

----------------------
Phase 1: The Ego Crash
----------------------

When he landed in the U.S., he thought:

* Good university
* Good brand
* Decent experience
* PM pivot will be manageable

Reality check?

150 applications → 0 offers
3 months → no interviews
Resume revised 15 times

This is where most people spiral.

Instead, we rebuilt from scratch.

---------------------------------------------------
Phase 2: Warm Networking (Strategic, Not Desperate)
---------------------------------------------------

Before most students even land, they start applying blindly.

He did something different.

He spoke to 40+ product managers before classes even started.

Not for referrals.

For intelligence.

He asked:

* When do PM internships open?
* How many does your company hire?
* What actually matters in screening?

He learned something brutal:

Some cohorts of 200 students had only 3 PM interns.

This changed his expectations.

This is why I tell Accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/r8ulr2p0neaoh3486e6c2hdnlgw33t7h365er/n2hohvhvm0x7eof6/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
) students: If you don’t know the hiring math, you are playing
blind.

------------------------------
Phase 3: Resume Identity Shift
------------------------------

He had a pure engineering resume.

99% model accuracy.
Published GitHub models.
Technical benchmarks.

Great engineer.
Wrong positioning.

We rebuilt it through a product lens.

Instead of:
“Improved model accuracy to 99%.”

It became:
“Improved model adoption by X%, reduced manual workflow by Y
hours weekly.”

Same work.
Different framing.
Different identity.

You must become the role before you get the role.

Most students try to “transition” without transforming.

That does not work anymore.

----------------------------------------------------
Phase 4: Post-Application Networking (The Real Edge)
----------------------------------------------------

Here’s what separated him.

After applying daily, he didn’t just wait.

He:

* Applied.
* Identified recruiter.
* Identified likely hiring manager.
* Sent 3-line email:* Who he is
* What value he brings
* Clear ask: “Would appreciate if you could review my
application.”

Every day.
3–5 targeted follow-ups.
For months.

Result?

Faster rejections.
Faster responses.
Actual traction.

One short email later helped move him from software screening to
product screening at the same company.

That email changed his career.

Most of you are applying.
Few of you are activating.

------------------
The Breaking Point
------------------

In January, after final-round rejection, he had a panic attack.

Not because of visa pressure.

Because expectations collapsed.

This is the invisible part no one posts on LinkedIn.

We talked about one thing:

“You are not failing. Your strategy is incomplete.”

So we pivoted.

He started applying to ML roles again as backup.

Confidence came back.

Offers started coming.

And something interesting happened…

When desperation left, performance improved.

He eventually landed:

* 3 offers
* 20+ interviews total
* 600+ applications
* 70+ mock interviews
* 1 product role from 1000 applicants

One seat.
He took it.

------------------
The Lesson For You
------------------

Stop romanticizing:

* Referrals
* Brand names
* Luck
* Right timing

Start engineering:

* Application velocity
* Post-application activation
* Resume identity alignment
* Interview reps

​Inside the Accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/r8ulr2p0neaoh3486e6c2hdnlgw33t7h365er/n2hohvhvm0x7eof6/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
), this is exactly what we build:

* Application tracking sheets
* Networking scripts
* Resume rewrites by role
* Mock interview drills
* Weekly execution accountability

Because mindset without mechanics is useless.

If you are serious about playing at this level,
You need systems, not hope.

More in the next newsletter - I’ll break down how he converted 1
seat out of 1000 applicants.

– Yudi J

P.S. If you’re already applying and not seeing traction, you
don’t need more motivation.
You need a strategy rebuild. That’s what we do inside the Job

Golang: The Random Chapters

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

    
    
    Read this article on LinkedIn to join the conversation
Read on LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/stop-guessing-start-measuring-benchmark-like-pro-golang-kumar-dlvec?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BaFvBRJN7QyiyFiohTjajNg%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=2SD7lbjSjYLY81&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mm8lmp45~ik-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mm8lmp45-ik
  
Every performance win I've ever shipped started the same way — not with clever code, but with honest numbers. This series is everything I wish someone handed me on day one of my golang coding. ① Foundations ② benchstat & Comparison ③ Memory & Allocations ④ Compiler Traps ⑤ Profiling & pprof "Measure twice and cut once." Ancient carpenters knew it. Every senior engineer learns it the hard way. In Go, the testing package is your tape measure. This article is about learning to use it right. I've spent the last decade reviewing Go performance PRs. The #1 mistake I see? Engineers optimizing code they've never benchmarked. They rewrite a perfectly fast function based on intuition, introduce subtle bugs, and end up with something 15% slower. Don't be that engineer. Let's build the right habits from the ground up — with the tools available in Go 1.24 on today's hardware. 🔬 The Battlefield: Modern Hardware Before we write a single line of benchmark code, we need to talk about the world your code runs in. In 2026, even a laptop has a 12-core CPU. Cloud servers run on Graviton4 or AMD EPYC with 192 hardware threads. This changes everything about how you think about performance. Modern CPUs have: aggressive branch prediction instruction pipelining multiple execution units turbo boost spikes up to ~40% This means your benchmark results can lie to you unless you know what to watch for. ⚠️ Thermal Throttling is Real On a laptop, your CPU might run at 4.2 GHz for the first 30 seconds, then throttle to 2.8 GHz. Your first benchmark run can be 30% faster than subsequent ones. Always discard the first run and use -count=10. 🧪 Setting Up a Stable Benchmark Environment Garbage in, garbage out. Here's what a serious benchmark environment looks like in 2026. ✅ Disable CPU frequency scaling (Linux) Set your CPU governor to performance: On macOS: plug in your charger — the OS handles this automatically. ✅ Pin to a specific CPU core Avoid core 0 (handles OS interrupts). This dramatically reduces variance. ✅ Close everything else Your browser, Slack, VS Code LSP — all of them introduce scheduler noise. For CI benchmarks: run in a dedicated container set CPU limits isolate workloads ✅ Commit to a baseline Go version Go 1.24 ships with improved GC and escape analysis. Benchmarks from Go 1.21 are not comparable. Lock your toolchain: 🚀 Your First Real Benchmark Let's skip recursive Fibonacci. Instead, we'll benchmark something that actually matters in real services: string building. We’ll compare three approaches engineers argue about every week. stringbuild/stringbuild.go 🧪 Writing the Benchmarks Every line matters. stringbuild/stringbuild_test.go ✨ New in Go 1.24: b.Loop() The old pattern: is gone. b.Loop() is cleaner, handles setup correctly, and avoids subtle bugs. Use it going forward. ▶️ Running the Benchmarks Example output: 🧠 How to Read This Like a Pro When you run Go benchmarks, the output is dense but incredibly revealing. Once you know how to read it, you start seeing performance stories instantly. Here is how to decode it like a senior engineer. 📊 Benchmark Output Example 🔍 Column-by-Column Breakdown BenchmarkBuildWithBuffer-8 This shows the benchmark name and the GOMAXPROCS value. The means Go used 8 logical CPUs This affects parallel behavior and scheduling Always note this when comparing runs 1483920 This is the number of iterations () the benchmark executed. What it tells you: Higher iteration count usually means the function is fast Go automatically adjusts this to get stable timing You usually do not compare this number directly across machines 808 ns/op This is the average time per operation — your primary latency metric. How to interpret: Lower is better This is wall-clock time per call Differences under ~5% may be noise without multiple runs Rule of thumb: Use and benchstat before declaring victory. 1280 B/op Average bytes allocated per operation. Why this matters more than many engineers think: Every allocation becomes future GC work High-throughput services amplify allocation costs Memory pressure often kills tail latency before raw CPU does Senior insight: A slightly slower function with far fewer allocations often wins in production. 2 allocs/op Number of distinct heap allocations per operation. This is your GC pressure indicator. Interpretation guide: → excellent, fully stack or reused → usually acceptable → investigate → almost always a red flag ⚡ Reading the Story Behind the Numbers Strong Go engineers do not just read the columns. They read the narrative. Ask yourself: Is time improving but allocations exploding? Is scaling linear across input sizes? Does performance collapse under parallel load? Is variance high across runs? Benchmarks are not just numbers. They are evidence. 🧭 Quick Mental Checklist Before trusting any benchmark: Was used? Was run? Is there a global sink preventing dead-code elimination? Was the first run discarded (thermal effects)? Are we comparing the same Go version? If any answer is “no,” treat the result with caution. Master this skill and you stop guessing. You start making performance decisions with confidence. 🔥 What the Numbers Reveal The naive concatenation approach is: ~12× slower 99 allocations per call Builder: 1 allocation dramatically lower GC pressure 💡 Golden Rule of Allocation: Every allocation is a future GC pause. On high-throughput services, reducing allocs/op is often more impactful than reducing ns/op. 📈 Sub-Benchmarks: Finding Where Complexity Hides Run: This reveals how your code actually scales. ✅ Benchmark Accuracy Checklist Print this and keep it near your monitor. Always use a global sink Always run with -benchmem Always use -count=10 Use sub-benchmarks for scaling Measure before you optimize Senior Go Engineer 10 years · High Performance Systems · Go Contributor I've shipped Go services processing millions of requests per second at companies you've heard of. I wrote this series because the best performance advice I know lives in Slack DMs and code review comments. It's time it lived somewhere everyone can find it. → Next in the series Part 2: benchstat — Stop Eyeballing Numbers, Start Having Conversations with Data In Part 2, we install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat, understand p-values and variance, do a real before/after comparison, and use the -benchtime=Nx trick to get deterministic results. Sprintax to help international students and professionals

US taxes.

​

If you are on F1, OPT, STEM OPT, or H1B, you are required to take
action, even if you did not earn income.

​

This session is designed to give you clarity on your residency
status, which forms apply to you, and how to avoid common
mistakes that can cost money or create unnecessary stress.

It is free to attend and purely educational.

​

If you are currently in the US on a visa, this is something you
should not ignore.

)
Register for webinar ( https://luma.com/qmqw41kx )
​
Now, let's start with newsletter....

Let’s do some math.

If you spend 2-3 hours tailoring a resume for each application…

And you apply to 40 roles…

That’s 80-120 hours.

That’s three full work weeks rewriting the same document.

Now here’s the uncomfortable question:

Did that effort increase your interview rate by 3x?

Usually, no.

Because the problem isn’t effort.
It’s structure.

Most job seekers operate in chaos mode:

* Open job description
* Panic
* Rewrite half the resume
* Second-guess everything
* Submit
* Repeat

That’s not strategy. That’s exhaustion.

In 2026 hiring, the winners aren’t the ones who tailor hardest.

They’re the ones who tailor intelligently.

Let’s break down a system that actually scales.

-----------------------------------------------------
First: Understand how recruiters read resumes in 2026
-----------------------------------------------------

Recruiters do not:

* Read every word
* Compare nuance
* Appreciate subtle phrasing

They:

* Scan title alignment
* Match keywords
* Confirm scope + impact
* Move on

You get ~20–30 seconds of attention.

Which means rewriting every bullet for every job is overkill.

What matters is surface alignment and search visibility. That’s
it.

--------------------------------------------------
The Leverage Model: 70% Foundation, 30% Adaptation
--------------------------------------------------

Instead of rewriting from scratch, build leverage.

Step 1: Create one master resume per target role
------------------------------------------------

Not one master resume overall.

One per role category.

Example:

* Backend Engineer resume
* Data Engineer resume
* Product Manager resume
* Technical Program Manager resume

Each version should:

* Reflect that title in the headline
* Prioritize relevant impact bullets
* Highlight the right technical stack
* Show business alignment for that role

Inside the accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/k0u59w0dvnf6h5rpgroulhor03qn0b8hd5738/kkhmh6hnrrl2v2al/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
), we never build “one universal resume.”
We build role-specific foundations.

Because relevance is contextual.

Step 2: Extract signal, not noise, from job descriptions
--------------------------------------------------------

Most people read the entire description line by line.

That’s inefficient.

Instead, look for patterns:

* Title
* First 5 responsibilities
* Required tools
* Seniority signals

Ignore company fluff.

You’re identifying:
"What would a recruiter type into search?"

If you see:
"Kubernetes, distributed systems, AWS, reliability"

Then your resume must reflect those exact terms if you have them.

Not synonyms.
Not creative rephrasing.
Direct alignment.

Step 3: Apply the 3-Point Adjustment Rule
-----------------------------------------

For each application, adjust only:

* Headline or summary line
* Skills section (if applicable)
* 1–2 bullets maximum

That’s it.

If the job emphasizes:
“Stakeholder management across GTM teams”

And your resume says:
“Collaborated cross-functionally”

Upgrade it.

Same truth.
Stronger signal.

Instead of:
“Improved user engagement metrics”

Try:
“Partnered with product and marketing to optimize onboarding,
increasing activation rate by 22%.”

You didn’t change your experience.
You clarified it.

This takes 5–10 minutes.
Not 2 hours.

------------------------------------------
The Compounding Advantage Most People Miss
------------------------------------------

Create a folder system:

Company Name – Role – Date

Every time you tailor intelligently, save it.

After 15–20 applications, you’ll notice something powerful:

Patterns.

You’ll see:

* Repeated keywords across similar roles
* Recurring expectations
* Gaps in your positioning

Now your tailoring gets faster.

This is how professionals scale applications without burning out.

-------------------------------------
Why over-tailoring actually hurts you
-------------------------------------

When you rewrite too much:

* You introduce inconsistencies
* You dilute your narrative
* You create identity confusion
* You slow your application velocity

And velocity matters.

Remember:
Interviews are influenced by timing + clarity.

Not perfection.

----------------------------
A Quick Analytical Framework
----------------------------

Ask yourself:

If I apply to 25 roles this month:

* How many convert to recruiter screens?
* What is my % conversion rate?
* Which resume version performs best?

If you’re not tracking this, you’re guessing.

Inside our office hour session (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/k0u59w0dvnf6h5rpgroulhor03qn0b8hd5738/kkhmh6hnrrl2v2al/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
), we often review:

* Resume version A vs version B
* Conversion data
* Keyword alignment

Because resume optimization should be iterative, not emotional.

-----------------------
Efficiency > Exhaustion
-----------------------

You don’t need to obsess.

You need to systemize.

Strong base.
Targeted tweaks.
Fast execution.
Data feedback.

That’s sustainable.

And sustainability wins in competitive markets.

If you want help building:

* Role-specific foundations

* Live feedback loops

Not resume decoration.

Before your next application, try this:

You’ll feel the difference immediately.

subject: 🚀 Level Up Your Build: How to Wow the Judges - Amazon Nova AI Hackathon
email_text:
( http://devpost.com )

Hey Builders!

As a veteran of more hackathons than we have fingers (and toes), we know the feeling. It’s 3:00 AM, the API is finally behaving, and you’re wondering: “How do I actually win this thing?” With a powerhouse model like Amazon Nova at your fingertips, the floor is high, but the ceiling is nonexistent. To move from "cool prototype" to "winner’s circle," you need to think like a judge. They aren’t just looking for code; they’re looking for a story, a solution, and a spark.

Here is your survival guide to standing out in the Amazon Nova Hackathon.

🧠 1. The Name: Give it a Soul
--------------------------------

Please, for the love of all things binary, don’t let an LLM name your project. 

*
The Tip: Pick a name that sounds like a real startup. Use a verb, an inside joke, or a metaphor.
*
Example: Instead of "Nova UI Automator," try "GhostCursor" or "SwiftStep."

📝 2. The Text Description: Sell the "Why"
--------------------------------------------

Judges might read your description before watching the video. If it’s just a list of libraries, you’ve lost them.

*
The Hook: Start with the problem. "Every day, 5,000 logistics managers struggle with X..."
*
The Nova Factor: Be specific about why Nova was the secret sauce. Don't forget to tell judges all the required tools you used.
*
Structure: Problem → Solution → Nova’s Role → Impact.

🎥 3. The Demo Video: The 3-Minute Masterpiece
------------------------------------------------

This is your "Shark Tank" moment. Use your 180 seconds wisely.

*
Show, Don't Just Tell: Don't spend 2 minutes on slides. Get to the UI/CLI within the first 30 seconds.
*
The "Golden Path": Show one clear, successful use case from start to finish.
*
Pro Tip (The "Fail-Safe"): If your live demo is prone to "demo demons," record a screen capture and voiceover it. It’s much cleaner than fumbling with a live mic.
*
New Tip: If you're doing Voice AI, show the user's reaction! Seeing a person interact naturally with Nova 2 Sonic is way more impactful than just hearing a waveform on a screen.
*
Don't forget: Include that #AmazonNova hashtag!

💻 4. The Code Repo: Don't Be a Mystery
-----------------------------------------

A messy repo says "I finished this 5 minutes ago." A clean repo says "I’m a pro."

*
The README is your resume: Include a clear Setup.md or a "Quick Start" section. If the judges can't get it running (or at least understand the architecture) quickly, they’ll move on.
*
(Optional if you have extra time) Architecture Diagram: Drop a simple diagram showing how Nova interacts with your agents or MCP tools. It proves you understand the "Agentic" part of the challenge.

🏆 5. The Bonus Prize: The "Builder" Advantage
------------------------------------------------

Don't skip the builder.aws.com blog post. It’s not just "extra credit"—it’s your chance to show the judges that your project has legs in the real world.

*
Focus on Community: Who does this help? A small business? Students? Doctors?
*
The Roadmap: Judges love to see that you’ve thought about "Day 2." How would you scale this?

⚡ Quick Tips for Each Category
--------------------------------

*
Agentic AI: Focus on reasoning. Show the agent making a decision or "pivoting" when it hits an obstacle.
*
Multimodal: Don't just "describe an image." Make Nova interpret something complex, like a handwritten note or a fast-paced video clip.
*
UI Automation (Nova Act): Choose a workflow that is notoriously annoying (like filling out 10-pages of forms) to maximize the "wow" factor.
*
Voice AI: Zero in on latency and tone. If it feels like a real conversation, you'll really stand out.

 

Final word of advice: Build something you actually want to exist. Your passion will show through in the demo.

Now, stop reading this and get back to building! We can’t wait to see what you create with Nova.

Purdue is expanding opportunities for Boilermakers at every stage of their careers. An enhanced lifelong learning initiative now offers 50 free online professional development courses for alumni, supporting continued growth in fast-evolving fields. Purdue is also deepening its research, industry and alumni engagement in Silicon Valley and growing its presence in Indianapolis with the launch of a master’s program in athletic training. Plus, a look back at the NFL Scouting Combine highlights how a Purdue team doctor helped bring the event to the city. Purdue expands lifelong learning portfolio to 50 free online courses for alumni  With workforce demands evolving quickly, Purdue is empowering alumni through an expanded slate of free, online professional development courses. Announced at the President’s Council meeting in Naples, Florida, the initiative — led by the Purdue for Life Foundation — now offers 50 courses across eight categories, from AI and technology to business and urban agriculture. READ MORE  Purdue brings 4 dimensions of engagement to Silicon Valley  Purdue recently announced a four-dimensional connection to Silicon Valley that deepens the university’s research and industry engagement through partnerships with leading technology companies. The presence of Purdue will also deepen engagement with the university’s large alumni community there. READ MORE  Watch: ‘Purdue News Now’ ▶️ Stay up to date with “Purdue News Now,” the one-minute video roundup of campus highlights. This week’s episode features Purdue’s expanding presence in Silicon Valley, free alumni lifelong learning courses, Mental Health Action Week on March 2-6 and more. WATCH Purdue master’s program in athletic training expands to Indianapolis location  Purdue’s athletic training program within the Department of Health and Kinesiology (HK) will expand its reach with a new Master of Science in Athletic Training degree for the Indianapolis location. The Indianapolis program will launch in fall 2026 with an expected cohort of 25-30 students. To train these new graduate students, HK will welcome three new faculty members to be based in Indianapolis. READ MORE  Why is the NFL combine in Indy? A Purdue team doctor played a role.  Do you know why the NFL Scouting Combine came to Indianapolis? According to Dr. Donald Shelbourne — former team physician at Purdue and with the Indianapolis Colts — it’s because the league learned that it could rely on the city’s unbeatable medical services during the predraft event. Learn how he and other Boilermaker medical professionals helped change how NFL teams collect prospects’ critical medical information ahead of the draft. READ MORE  Boiler crossword Purdue fans can snag the jerseys of basketball greats thanks to the new Boilermaker Legends Collection. After you shop the icons of Mackey Arena, see if you can put up a legendary performance on this week’s crossword. share with you..

​

I am hosting a free live tax session in collaboration with
Sprintax to help international students and professionals
understand what they are actually required to file for their 2025
US taxes.

​

If you are on F1, OPT, STEM OPT, or H1B, you are required to take
action, even if you did not earn income.

​

This session is designed to give you clarity on your residency
status, which forms apply to you, and how to avoid common
mistakes that can cost money or create unnecessary stress.

​

It is free to attend and purely educational.

​

If you are currently in the US on a visa, this is something you
should not ignore.

​

-->Register for webinar (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/xmuwgx7mnks6hpoq5z5c5h2d4v7gganhdxogk/owhkhqhwpx75qwhv/aHR0cHM6Ly9sdW1hLmNvbS9xbXF3NDFreA==
)
Register for webinar ( https://luma.com/qmqw41kx )
​
Now, let's start with newsletter....

Let’s do some math.

If you spend 2-3 hours tailoring a resume for each application…

And you apply to 40 roles…

That’s 80-120 hours.

That’s three full work weeks rewriting the same document.

Now here’s the uncomfortable question:

Did that effort increase your interview rate by 3x?

Usually, no.

Because the problem isn’t effort.
It’s structure.

Most job seekers operate in chaos mode:

* Open job description
* Panic
* Rewrite half the resume
* Second-guess everything
* Submit
* Repeat

That’s not strategy. That’s exhaustion.

In 2026 hiring, the winners aren’t the ones who tailor hardest.

They’re the ones who tailor intelligently.

Let’s break down a system that actually scales.

-----------------------------------------------------
First: Understand how recruiters read resumes in 2026
-----------------------------------------------------

Recruiters do not:

* Read every word
* Compare nuance
* Appreciate subtle phrasing

They:

* Scan title alignment
* Match keywords
* Confirm scope + impact
* Move on

You get ~20–30 seconds of attention.

Which means rewriting every bullet for every job is overkill.

What matters is surface alignment and search visibility. That’s
it.

--------------------------------------------------
The Leverage Model: 70% Foundation, 30% Adaptation
--------------------------------------------------

Instead of rewriting from scratch, build leverage.

Step 1: Create one master resume per target role
------------------------------------------------

Not one master resume overall.

One per role category.

Example:

* Backend Engineer resume
* Data Engineer resume
* Product Manager resume
* Technical Program Manager resume

Each version should:

* Reflect that title in the headline
* Prioritize relevant impact bullets
* Highlight the right technical stack
* Show business alignment for that role

Inside the accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/xmuwgx7mnks6hpoq5z5c5h2d4v7gganhdxogk/z2hghnhen580lpip/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
), we never build “one universal resume.”
We build role-specific foundations.

Because relevance is contextual.

Step 2: Extract signal, not noise, from job descriptions
--------------------------------------------------------

Most people read the entire description line by line.

That’s inefficient.

Instead, look for patterns:

* Title
* First 5 responsibilities
* Required tools
* Seniority signals

Ignore company fluff.

You’re identifying:
"What would a recruiter type into search?"

If you see:
"Kubernetes, distributed systems, AWS, reliability"

Then your resume must reflect those exact terms if you have them.

Not synonyms.
Not creative rephrasing.
Direct alignment.

Step 3: Apply the 3-Point Adjustment Rule
-----------------------------------------

For each application, adjust only:

* Headline or summary line
* Skills section (if applicable)
* 1–2 bullets maximum

That’s it.

If the job emphasizes:
“Stakeholder management across GTM teams”

And your resume says:
“Collaborated cross-functionally”

Upgrade it.

Same truth.
Stronger signal.

Instead of:
“Improved user engagement metrics”

Try:
“Partnered with product and marketing to optimize onboarding,
increasing activation rate by 22%.”

You didn’t change your experience.
You clarified it.

This takes 5–10 minutes.
Not 2 hours.

------------------------------------------
The Compounding Advantage Most People Miss
------------------------------------------

Create a folder system:

Company Name – Role – Date

Every time you tailor intelligently, save it.

After 15–20 applications, you’ll notice something powerful:

Patterns.

You’ll see:

* Repeated keywords across similar roles
* Recurring expectations
* Gaps in your positioning

Now your tailoring gets faster.

This is how professionals scale applications without burning out.

-------------------------------------
Why over-tailoring actually hurts you
-------------------------------------

When you rewrite too much:

* You introduce inconsistencies
* You dilute your narrative
* You create identity confusion
* You slow your application velocity

And velocity matters.

Remember:
Interviews are influenced by timing + clarity.

Not perfection.

----------------------------
A Quick Analytical Framework
----------------------------

Ask yourself:

If I apply to 25 roles this month:

* How many convert to recruiter screens?
* What is my % conversion rate?
* Which resume version performs best?

If you’re not tracking this, you’re guessing.

Inside our office hour session (
https://604b57c3.click.kit-mail3.com/xmuwgx7mnks6hpoq5z5c5h2d4v7gganhdxogk/z2hghnhen580lpip/aHR0cHM6Ly9hY2FkZW15Lnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9qb2JodW50bmw=
), we often review:

* Resume version A vs version B
* Conversion data
* Keyword alignment

Because resume optimization should be iterative, not emotional.

-----------------------
Efficiency > Exhaustion
-----------------------

You don’t need to obsess.

You need to systemize.

Strong base.
Targeted tweaks.
Fast execution.
Data feedback.

That’s sustainable.

And sustainability wins in competitive markets.

Hey there —
 
It’s been a busy few weeks at Clerk, with updates across analytics, billing, AI tooling, and more. If you haven’t checked the
changelog lately, here’s a quick look at what’s new.
 


New pricing and plans that deliver more value

Clerk’s first major pricing update in years is here and it includes more free retained users, unlimited applications on every
plan, bundled essentials like MFA and simultaneous sessions, and automatic volume discounts.
 



 
Now growing teams get more headroom by default without needing to constantly rethink their pricing tier. Read more →
[https://go.clerk.com/u1lAYtV]




Visualize individual user activity with the new User Activity report

You can now see how often a specific user engages with your product over time via the new User Activity report, right from their
profile page.
 



 
See how often a user is active and catch engagement patterns before they become churn. Read more → [https://go.clerk.com/Vd8XdlX]




Clerk Skills: teach AI agents to help you build with Clerk

Introducing Clerk Skills, installable packages that give AI coding assistants specialized Clerk auth knowledge. Once installed,
your AI agent can help add auth flows, sync users to your database, build custom sign-in screens, and more.
 



 
Spend less time fixing auth flows and more time shipping features with AI tools that understand your auth layer. Read more →
[https://go.clerk.com/VvSUoh5]




Custom billing plans and smooth subscription transitions

Clerk Billing now supports transitioning active subscriptions between plans and prices directly from the Dashboard or API. You can
manage upgrades, downgrades, and promotional pricing without building custom logic.
 



 
No more handling plan migrations manually. Read more → [https://go.clerk.com/RzJL7dD]




Export Dashboard analytics to share insights

Charts in your Clerk Dashboard can now be exported as high-quality images or copied to your clipboard, perfect for sharing trends
with teammates, stakeholders, or on social.
 



 
Share more than just screenshots, get polished metrics in seconds. Read more → [https://go.clerk.com/DexgKQK]




Org Retention Chart

You can now track retention at the organization level, not just individual users. This gives you visibility into how teams engage
with your product over time.
 



 
Understand retention at the account level, not just per user.




Other features, fixes, and improvements

 * iOS & Android SDK v1 [https://go.clerk.com/5MEI5dJ] — Native SDKs, unified auth surface.

 * Require MFA [https://go.clerk.com/NzzZxHA] — Enforce stronger security with one toggle.

 * Enterprise connection testing [https://go.clerk.com/7C2dGrk] — Shareable SSO test links with logs.

 * Improved Stripe account detection [https://go.clerk.com/joTe8le] — Proactive Stripe status warnings.

 
Everything's live and waiting for you.
 
Keep shipping.
 
– Emily at Clerk

The HireReady Newsletter Vol. 82: The Art of the Career Heist

Feeling like you're playing a game with no rules? I see you, and I know how frustrating the job search can be. This week, we're ditching the old playbook and pulling off a "Career Heist" - a series of clever, unexpected moves to get you into the career you deserve.

🛠️ The job search hacks 🛠️

🔮 Use the Job Tracker to Predict the Future 🔮

Instead of just using the Jobscan Job Tracker to keep tabs on where you've applied, we're going to use it as a crystal ball. By tracking not just your applications, but also interesting job postings for roles you might want in the future, you can start to see patterns in the required skills and qualifications. This allows you to spot emerging trends and upskill before the perfect job even appears.

Next Steps

First, start saving a wider range of job descriptions to your Job Tracker, even for roles a level or two above your current target. Second, once a week, review the "Skills" and "Keywords" sections of these tracked jobs. Third, look for commonalities and outliers. These are your clues to what skills will be most valuable in your field in the next 6-12 months, giving you a head start on the competition.

Use Job Tracker for Free
(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VVtHP_1B3trlW6__57D6ck7vtW4bWRWk5K_x26N1c6sqP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3mQW5jKMrV7NGD3lW1fQxxx36BYy4W3HtcNp6Pn_T7W4h9r0J8Y7m81N4RHHvBPBpgkV7M8y-6G2JzHW3Nz7BG4KmlPyW5wRF_f1nKgG9VZQ_xb4LgGnZW35dC_L92k5gLW6F34wW282CJ2W66HKty6pN5rcW477l1l8rcX_MN7LVyW0R_MjmW7JVl8H36trjQW6kY_8N3kvLtSV10QQH9glQ5pW4NxsF14BRjc4V3nYt7344K3wW91xzfy51TlR3W3BbcMz5zgrN_W2YHfDq27M_czW515dJn95Nc2hW3Ksjjv51Wwy-f5WdJd404 )

⏳ The Informational Interview "Time Bomb" ⏳

Everyone tells you to do informational interviews to gather information. We're going to do them to plant seeds. The goal isn't just to learn about a company; it's to create a network of advocates who will think of you when a role opens up. The "time bomb" is the meticulously planned follow-up that keeps you top-of-mind.

Next Steps

First, identify 5-10 people at companies you admire and reach out for brief informational chats. Second, during the conversation, ask insightful questions about their challenges and the company's goals. Third, set a reminder to follow up every 4-6 weeks with a relevant article, a quick update on your own progress, or a note of congratulations on a company achievement you saw in the news. You're not asking for a job; you're building a genuine connection that will pay off later.

(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VVtHP_1B3trlW6__57D6ck7vtW4bWRWk5K_x26N1c6srn3gP0xW8wLKSR6lZ3pTN2HYnP7ZPFPvW3MSXlv9jK-LvVGZPsz98bFxpW41qZsS1Kt-rWW4Qq3Gz8nYCC1W4v5Pdc4Gw_j8W1hlcZR1b9hWwW3cdv453Nm4QSW4wSBj33FpKs9N7J4rzHbPW9nW6VxDBY3rSbwRW8glHRl6ldN1cW21b0JG5BmMrBW6tg5D58jNlS8W2Mv7FC7wYxHvW8Cp7pb8VHht0W2b0Rv52w9D4rW6q459v7-t4jkW7SSPHf8PsDSYW5vMXW02CB0zQW32HqjW91lgs6W4mWqsJ7LDm0nW4cz9j86TKQzfN843LYLC1KkKW6VLRKL1DHCt7W5SwM3y2NfHk4W89Nxdn5g1T8bN1sjgJXb0s3Df7WZqrK04 )

🛠️ Reverse-Engineer Your Career Path 🛠️

Stop guessing what it takes to land your dream job and start working with a proven blueprint. Instead of just looking at job descriptions, you're going to become a detective and study the career trajectories of people who currently hold the roles you want. This will give you a much more realistic and actionable roadmap.

Next Steps

First, find 10-15 people on LinkedIn who have the job title you're aiming for at companies that interest you. Second, analyze their career histories. What skills did they acquire? What kinds of roles did they have before their current one? Did they get any specific certifications? Third, look for common patterns in their paths and use this "reverse-engineered" blueprint to inform your own career development and job search strategy.

Tool: Optimize your LinkedIn profile for your job search
(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VVtHP_1B3trlW6__57D6ck7vtW4bWRWk5K_x26N1c6sqP3gP0xW7lCdLW6lZ3pcN7MLQLVxxSp0W8WYYZj8B4bGjW47V7cw45FL2wW76LLWj6B23pCW2xQcZ97_srf2VLNbv23-cCkvW2w2zVP3v7xqXW6ymTqb4yzwqVW64WDY74TvN7rW3F4bpN7-xsCJVJMKrv1t4qNKW6KgKpw4BTfv-W8Sd-0W5q3wRrW3b34ZB2XZbq4W33pcFk9cx1bcW1Lsy-F3X8tt4W6lKTZM3n8KsQW4ks6_S28dCRPW71cN5P7DwzRLW2y2hs47KTXXKW3GG8kf52xMMKW1K-Jh031FjThVXG1Fb3f-FLMW3dB-Zq2FXPJZf2Klrhb04 )

👀 Become a Company Culture Insider 👀

The best way to ace an interview is to show you already "get" the company culture. You're going to go beyond a cursory glance at their website and become a temporary insider. This will allow you to speak their language and align your answers with their core values in a way that feels authentic and impressive.

Next Steps

First, spend an hour immersing yourself in the company's online presence. Read their blog, watch their videos, and analyze the tone and language of their social media posts. Second, search for recent news articles and press releases to understand their current priorities and challenges. Third, look up the company on Glassdoor and other review sites to get a sense of the employee experience. Weave these insights into your interview answers to show you've done your homework and are a perfect fit.

Guide: Learn how to research a company before your interview
(https://info.jobscan.co/e3t/Ctc/S+113/cvzDf04/VVtHP_1B3trlW6__57D6ck7vtW4bWRWk5K_x26N1c6sr43gP0xW7Y8-PT6lZ3lMW3GsBMg48Gl_kW3JwyVj8kKt3KW4fmhjG7V1T3tW7bM0_N74kfSsW3w1pYk2F0cCSW2gGVtF3jl56cW5XqFcq7j3-M3W1xVb784RH1P4W6l9nyT544-hNW80hCsQ7W5NLmW7XmGkh6K52nJW1grBbf4NVJ-7W4BrgSh4wDsL8MDz6bwWh7TpW3YWVr62Y2KH7W2V_pS83Pd-_YN5mJw7vNgg38W5D0r8t5MmN0LW8s0HYF5Lf66cW4s2HXc3VCZbBW78jsrS8mS0N_W6ZVp524Hs8kXW4X_RxT3lXVs7W7xfs8_7wqgKXW27s-XJ5QQ9MqW3lkc6c4rzXhyf6PZD6W04 )

Remember, the "Career Heist" isn't about taking something that isn't yours; it's about being clever and strategic to claim the career that has your name on it. This week, I encourage you to pick just one of these hacks and give it a try. You might be surprised at what you can unlock with a little unconventional thinking. You've got this.

subject: In case you missed: How she got Tesla, Walmart, Zipline offers
email_text:
Hi Nandini,
Yudi here.

I recently recorded a podcast with Venonshya (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/zluv2lkeqxunhknq3qeiphwgqvr8ku6hk0vr8/x0hph6heox8rdpt5/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_dD0yOHMmdj1VdkFnTUJNNEp6Yw==
), and what stood out was not the number of offers she got.

It was how methodical her approach was.

She landed in the US in August and by September she had already
started applying.
Not waiting for a "perfect resume."
Not waiting to feel ready.
She iterated while applying.

Within 3 months, she had interviews and offers from Tesla,
Walmart, and Zipline for technical program and automation roles.

She had no prior PM or TPM title.

What Actually Worked in Her Job Hunt

1. Consistency beat intensity

She didn’t apply in bursts.
She applied every single day.
5 to 10 applications. Tracked. Reviewed. Improved.
Even on days packed with assignments.

2. She separated "getting interviews" from "cracking interviews"

Venonshya believes getting the interview is the hardest part.
Once she had one, she went deep.

She researched the company’s technology, products, and recent
launches.
At Tesla, she discussed their product roadmap and industry
direction instead of generic answers.
That shifted the interview from Q&A to conversation.

3. She prepared stories before anyone asked

She maintained a separate document where every resume bullet was
expanded using the STAR method.
Situation. Task. Action. Result.
So when interviews came, she wasn’t improvising.

4. She treated networking as learning, not asking

She reached out to people on LinkedIn to understand roles, not to
immediately ask for referrals.
Coffee chats helped her understand how TPM roles differ across
Tesla, Walmart, and Zipline.
That clarity shaped how she answered interviews and which roles
she pursued.

Where Purdue MEM Actually Fit In

Venonshya was a Purdue Master’s in Engineering Management (MEM)
student (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/zluv2lkeqxunhknq3qeiphwgqvr8ku6hk0vr8/6qheh8hlz0vk6who/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9wdXJkdWVtZW0=
) when all of this happened.

That mattered.

Not because Purdue “guarantees” outcomes, but how early the
program pushes career readiness.

Within the first few weeks on campus, she was already iterating
on her resume, speaking with seniors, and getting feedback from
the career advisory team.

Purdue MEM helped her translate engineering work into program and
product language.
- Cross-functional experience.
- Quantified impact.
- Clear ownership stories.

She also benefited from Purdue’s industry exposure.
Sessions with companies like Tesla, Walmart, and others gave
students visibility into how hiring actually works and what
interviewers look for beyond keywords.

That combination - early preparation, structured feedback, and a
strong engineering brand - gave her a real shot when
opportunities came up.

The effort was hers.
The environment helped make that effort count.

What 2026 Aspirants Can Take From This

If you’re planning a master’s in Fall 2026 and targeting TPM,
automation, or engineering-adjacent roles:

• Start resume and LinkedIn prep before landing
• Apply early, not perfectly
• Treat interview prep as a separate skill
• Research companies deeply, not broadly
• Use coffee chats to learn roles, not chase referrals
• Choose programs where career prep starts early and stays
consistent

Venonshya’s journey is proof that preparation compounds quietly.

subject: How she got Tesla, Walmart, Zipline offers
email_text:
Hi Nandini,
Yudi here.

I recently recorded a podcast with Venonshya (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/d0uwx849d7s0hovg355cmhz2qrzkpflh0ve7p/reh8hohm4wlroxi2/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_dD0yOHMmdj1VdkFnTUJNNEp6Yw==
), and what stood out was not the number of offers she got.

It was how methodical her approach was.

She landed in the US in August and by September she had already
started applying.
Not waiting for a "perfect resume."
Not waiting to feel ready.
She iterated while applying.

Within 3 months, she had interviews and offers from Tesla,
Walmart, and Zipline for technical program and automation roles.

She had no prior PM or TPM title.

What Actually Worked in Her Job Hunt

1. Consistency beat intensity

She didn’t apply in bursts.
She applied every single day.
5 to 10 applications. Tracked. Reviewed. Improved.
Even on days packed with assignments.

2. She separated "getting interviews" from "cracking interviews"

Venonshya believes getting the interview is the hardest part.
Once she had one, she went deep.

She researched the company’s technology, products, and recent
launches.
At Tesla, she discussed their product roadmap and industry
direction instead of generic answers.
That shifted the interview from Q&A to conversation.

3. She prepared stories before anyone asked

She maintained a separate document where every resume bullet was
expanded using the STAR method.
Situation. Task. Action. Result.
So when interviews came, she wasn’t improvising.

4. She treated networking as learning, not asking

She reached out to people on LinkedIn to understand roles, not to
immediately ask for referrals.
Coffee chats helped her understand how TPM roles differ across
Tesla, Walmart, and Zipline.
That clarity shaped how she answered interviews and which roles
she pursued.

Where Purdue MEM Actually Fit In

Venonshya was a Purdue Master’s in Engineering Management (MEM)
student (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/d0uwx849d7s0hovg355cmhz2qrzkpflh0ve7p/8ghqhohozq6v7wuk/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9wdXJkdWVtZW0=
) when all of this happened.

That mattered.

Not because Purdue “guarantees” outcomes, but how early the
program pushes career readiness.

Within the first few weeks on campus, she was already iterating
on her resume, speaking with seniors, and getting feedback from
the career advisory team.

Purdue MEM helped her translate engineering work into program and
product language.
- Cross-functional experience.
- Quantified impact.
- Clear ownership stories.

She also benefited from Purdue’s industry exposure.
Sessions with companies like Tesla, Walmart, and others gave
students visibility into how hiring actually works and what
interviewers look for beyond keywords.

That combination - early preparation, structured feedback, and a
strong engineering brand - gave her a real shot when
opportunities came up.

The effort was hers.
The environment helped make that effort count.

What 2026 Aspirants Can Take From This

If you’re planning a master’s in Fall 2026 and targeting TPM,
automation, or engineering-adjacent roles:

• Start resume and LinkedIn prep before landing
• Apply early, not perfectly
• Treat interview prep as a separate skill
• Research companies deeply, not broadly
• Use coffee chats to learn roles, not chase referrals
• Choose programs where career prep starts early and stays
consistent

Venonshya’s journey is proof that preparation compounds quietly.

Watch the full podcast with Venonshya → Watch here (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/d0uwx849d7s0hovg355cmhz2qrzkpflh0ve7p/reh8hohm4wlroxi2/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_dD0yOHMmdj1VdkFnTUJNNEp6Yw==
)​

If you’re an someone looking to turn into a decision-maker,

opens doors while you’re still studying. Check them out here. (

World-renowned plant geneticist Gebisa Ejeta will be inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for research that advanced global food security and helped save millions from starvation. His pioneering research of the grain sorghum produced drought- and disease-resistant hybrids, boosted yields and helped save millions from starvation while advancing global food security, particularly across Africa. ( http://devpost.com )

Whether or not you have started building your GitLab AI Hackathon project, the GitLab Discord ( https://discord.com/invite/gitlab ) #ai-hackathon channel and Devpost’s Discord Community ( https://discord.gg/GS92Wtq2wS ) are the perfect communities to connect with other developers! Not only can you bounce ideas off each other and ask other developers for technical help, but you can also use it to ask GitLab and Devpost teams questions and eventually show off your project when it’s finished!

🤝 Teaming up

Looking for a team to work with on your project? Post in the Discord channel! You can also use the challenge Participants Tab ( https://gitlab.devpost.com/participants ) to search for other developers looking to team up, check out their skills and message them to see if they want to collaborate.

Visit the Participants tab ( https://gitlab.devpost.com/participants ) to see other participants of the competition on Devpost. subject: 💕 February Replit Product Updates
email_text:
Production database access for Agent, Agent Inbox, & more.



 <https://replit.com>



Friday, February 20, 2026


Hi, I don’t believe we’ve met! I’m Sarah, the new DevRel at Replit. It’s so 
nice to meet you :)

Here’s what we shipped in the first two weeks of February:


 * Agent can securely query your production SQL database (read-only)
 * Agent Inbox for collecting and implementing live user feedback

and many more! Let's dive in.




🗄️ Agent + Your Production Database 



Now you can ask Agent questions about what your users are actually seeing.

Agent can now securely view and query your production SQL database in 
read-only mode.

That means you can:


 *  Debug issues against real user data
 * Understand live schemas instantly
 * Build features with real production context

No risk of accidental writes, just smarter decisions powered by real data.

For teams shipping production apps, this is a major win!


📬 Agent Inbox 



 Your users can now leave feedback directly on your published apps, and Agent 
can implement it.

When someone submits feedback through the built-in widget, it appears in your 
Agent Inbox 
<https://docs.replit.com/cloud-services/deployments/enable-feedback?utm_source=iterable&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=replit-product-updates>
. From there, you can prompt Agent to make the requested improvements.

 I just added this feature to my own apps!


📌 Other new features


 * Open in Replit (Linear Beta) – Open Linear tickets directly in Replit with 
issue details automatically prefilled in your prompt
 * Custom OpenAI key support (Teams) – Use your own OpenAI API key instead of 
the default model provider 

 You can find weekly updates and more in our changelog 
<https://docs.replit.com/updates>.


📹 Videos

Ambitious builders treat addition like oxygen. More goals. More inputs. More tools. More options. It registers as drive. The system registers dilution. The quiet failure mode is not insufficient effort. It is reflexive accumulation. Effort stays high. Trajectory flattens. This is the inversion most miss. 1️⃣ Weekly Signal — Growth Is Dying Under Excess Ambitious operators accumulate by default. Environments reward visible motion, FOMO, and the status of “doing more.” New layers feel productive. Excess multiplies variables until causality disappears. What moved the needle becomes untraceable. Calendars overflow. Output remains linear. You log the hours, yet the compounding curve refuses to bend. 2️⃣ What Excess Actually Does 1. Excess inputs → fragmented attention. Constant context switches prevent deep pattern recognition and synthesis. 2. Excess projects → diluted feedback. Parallel bets make causal attribution impossible; no single loop ever tightens. 3. Excess tools → shallow mastery. Onboarding tax and novelty bias keep every instrument at surface level. 3️⃣ The Reduction Model Acceleration follows this exact sequence: 1. Subtract non-core variables until only the highest-signal axis remains. 2. Isolate that axis completely. 3. Compress feedback cycles to near-instant. 4. Protect the narrowed system from re-accumulation. Reduction creates clarity. Clarity sharpens feedback. Rapid feedback ignites compounding. 4️⃣ Turn It Into Leverage Apply these rules this week: Cut: The single project or input surviving purely on momentum. Commit: One vertical domain for uninterrupted 90-day focus—no lateral experiments. Refuse: Any new optimization or tool that adds complexity without proven 5x leverage in your current system. The durable principle: Mastery compounds in subtraction, never addition. next issue next week ...

Hi Nandini,
Yudi here.

Every week, I hear some version of this:

“The system filtered me out.”
“The ATS didn’t like my resume.”
“I need to beat the algorithm.”

Let me say this clearly in 2026:

The ATS is not your enemy.

It’s not a sentient gatekeeper deciding your fate.

It’s a searchable database.

And databases don’t reject people.
They return results.

If you’re not getting callbacks, it’s usually because of two
things:

* You applied after the shortlist was forming.
* Your resume doesn’t match what recruiters are actually
searching for.

Let’s break this down properly.

https://kitads.link/a8531279d8/1320154/8607 )

-----------------------------------
What an ATS actually does (in 2026)
-----------------------------------

An ATS today still does three core things:

• Stores resumes
• Allows recruiters to search using keywords
• Tracks candidates through stages

Yes, some platforms layer AI ranking on top.
But the foundation hasn’t changed:

Recruiters open the system.
They type keywords.
They skim the first batch of matches.

You either appear in that search…
or you don’t.

There’s no dramatic rejection moment.

If your resume doesn’t contain the terms they’re filtering for,
you simply never surface.

That’s not sabotage. That’s indexing.

----------------------------------------
The timing problem no one wants to admit
----------------------------------------

Here’s what I’m seeing in 2026 hiring cycles:

• Roles are reviewed in waves.
• First 24–72 hours matter most.
• Shortlists are often formed within the first week.

If you apply on day 6 or 7, you’re not being rejected because
you’re unqualified.

You’re competing with momentum that already exists.

Inside our Job Hunting Accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/75uroqn826h8h6ql852szhwrrmr66bnhn3pk7/08he4w5wh9h2vmpmd3ul/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
), one of the first shifts we make is this:

Stop chasing jobs. Start tracking companies.

Our members set alerts directly on company career pages and apply
when listings go live, not when they trend on LinkedIn three days
later.

​Watch this video (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/75uroqn826h8h6ql852szhwrrmr66bnhn3pk7/z2hghnhenomo3lap/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cueW91dHViZS5jb20vd2F0Y2g_dj00OTBBNUNTVjNzNA==
) to know the exact steps.

This change alone improves interview conversion dramatically.

--------------------------
The keyword mismatch issue
--------------------------

Most tech professionals don’t have weak resumes.

They have mismatched resumes.

Let’s say a recruiter searches:

“Senior Backend Engineer” + “Kubernetes” + “microservices” +
“AWS”

​

If your resume says:

“Cloud-native distributed systems deployment” but never
explicitly says “Kubernetes”

You don’t appear in the search.

Because you didn’t mirror language.

This isn’t about stuffing buzzwords.

It’s about precision.

​

Instead of:

“Improved platform scalability across services”

Try:

“Scaled Kubernetes-based microservices architecture on AWS,
improving system throughput by 35%.”

One reads like effort.
The other reads like a match.

In our resume review sessions (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/75uroqn826h8h6ql852szhwrrmr66bnhn3pk7/25hpokk9foh367q72kt3/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
), this is where most rewrites happen - not formatting tweaks,
but alignment fixes.

---------------------------------------
Think like the recruiter for 30 seconds
---------------------------------------

Here’s the mental shift that changes everything.

Imagine you are the recruiter.

You open the ATS and search:

“Product Manager” + “B2B SaaS” + “roadmap” + “stakeholder
management”

The system shows 40 resumes.

You click the first 10 that clearly match the search terms.

You do not:
• read every resume deeply
• analyze potential
• decode vague language

You scan for relevance.

If your headline says:

“Strategic leader with cross-functional experience”

You disappear.

If it says:

“Product Manager | B2B SaaS | Roadmap & Go-to-Market Execution”

You surface.

Same person.
Different visibility.

------------------------
What’s different in 2026
------------------------

Hiring tech teams are leaner.
Recruiters manage more reqs per headcount.
Search filters are tighter.

That means:

Clarity > creativity
Precision > personality
Relevance > storytelling (at the first stage)

Storytelling matters in interviews.
Searchability matters before that.

This is why we don’t just help people “improve resumes” inside
the accelerator.

We help them build:
• Search-aligned resumes
• Modular keyword blocks
• Role-specific summaries
• Timing systems

And then we review them live during office hours so you’re not
guessing.

----------------------------------------
A simple 2026 checklist before you apply
----------------------------------------

Before submitting your next application, check:

□ Does my title match the role exactly?
□ Do I mirror 5-7 core skills from the job description?
□ Are those keywords in my headline, summary, and at least 2
bullets?
□ Am I applying within the first 72 hours?

If not, you’re relying on hope. And hope is not a strategy.

The ATS isn’t rejecting you. Recruiters can’t consider what they
can’t find.

Your goal isn’t to outsmart a system. It’s to show up clearly
inside it.

And if you want structured help with:
• Resume alignment
• Keyword optimization
• Timing strategy
• Office-hour feedback
• Masterclasses with hiring managers

That’s exactly why the Job Hunting Accelerator (
https://604b57c3.click.convertkit-mail2.com/75uroqn826h8h6ql852szhwrrmr66bnhn3pk7/08he4w5wh9h2vmpmd3ul/aHR0cHM6Ly9saW5rLnl1ZGlqLmNvbS9uZXdzbGV0dGVyZW1haWw=
) exists.

The market is competitive.

But it’s not mysterious.

You just need to understand how visibility works.

— Yudi J

Dear HDFC Bank Customer, 

Fraudsters are sending WhatsApp messages pretending to be from the RTO, with fake challan alerts. These messages contain APK links. If installed, these apps silently infect your phone. 

Fraudsters can then access your screen, NetBanking, read your OTPs, forward calls and SMS, misuse your personal information, access your WhatsApp and can even apply for Loans or Credit in your name.  

To stay protected from such frauds, follow these safe practices: 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Do not click on links or attachments  from unknown senders. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Verify challan details only via the official RTO portal:  https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=te447b6d5-7158-4961-95f5-1cbf5f1b24be,23bb94,a8d3d parivahan.gov.in 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Use antivirus or anti-malware apps and update them regularly. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Report suspicious messages on the Chakshu portal: 

 https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=te447b6d5-7158-4961-95f5-1cbf5f1b24be,23bb94,a8d3e sancharsaathi.gov.in  or via the Sanchar Saathi mobile app. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

If you’ve fallen victim to such fraud, immediately contact your bank. 

You can also file a complaint at  https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=te447b6d5-7158-4961-95f5-1cbf5f1b24be,23bb94,a8d3f cybercrime.gov.in  or call 1930.

As AI accelerates from experimentation to enterprise backbone, new research shows a widening gap between AI ambition and actual financial return: 👉 Only 25% of AI initiatives deliver expected ROI. 👉 Only 16% of AI initiatives scale enterprise‑wide. The message is clear: AI isn’t failing, deployment strategies are.  Our new ROI playbook outlines a roadmap for those needing to turn AI investments into measurable business impact. Read more for insights on how AI‑first leaders are actually driving ROI. Plus, learn more about our newest AI advancements. ⤵ 1. Start with cost savings, then scale up 💡 The most successful AI programs begin with cost‑focused use cases, delivering measurable wins quickly and building momentum for larger transformation. Examples include: Automating document analysis to reduce analyst workload and improve decision accuracy. Streamlining claims processing to improve payouts, customer satisfaction, and scalability without adding headcount.  These grounded, repeatable use cases establish credibility, and resources, to scale AI strategically. 2. Choose high-impact use cases 🎯 The playbook warns against distributing AI across the enterprise without focus. Instead, tech leaders should target clear, high-value workflows, such as: Repetitive tasks (claims, data entry) Manual handoffs across systems Work requiring complex policy interpretation Processes burdened by high operational cost or inefficiency See how AI-driven business growth starts with a clear strategy ⤵ 3. Establish a baseline before you measure ROI 📊 One of the most common pitfalls: measuring AI success without understanding the starting point. We emphasize baselining performance, cost, and workflows as a prerequisite to demonstrating ROI credibly. This helps leaders communicate success, secure budget, and justify expansion. 👉 Unlock the rest of the insights here Industry assessments As leaders push for measurable outcomes, the conversation around AI is shifting from experimentation to accountability. That’s why it’s worth exploring how industry analysts are assessing AI’s impact today. The Economist shares how AI is reshaping enterprise performance and what separates organizations extracting real value from those still struggling to scale. "At a time when an estimated 95% of companies are not seeing an ROI on their AI investments, I'm confident that IBM is part of the 5% that is succeeding - and we're helping our clients do the same." - Mohamad Ali, SVP & Head of IBM Consulting Here's why The Economist thinks we had a striking turnaround → https://ibm.biz/BdprPy

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

Read on LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/go-lied-you-equality-would-have-believed-abhishek-kumar-hwp5c?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BMMHiCvHzSiuhsHqFye969A%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=2Ow6WVwn65vs81&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mlrpta5y~il-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mlrpta5y-il
  
A short story about pointers, memory, and why returning &value should make your nose wrinkle Let me show you a program. Read it carefully. Answer honestly. Alice lives in London. Bob lives in London. Both were set from the exact same constant — LONDON. Are their cities equal? ... The program prints false. Wait. What? I know. Your brain screamed "true". Mine did too. Here's the thing: City() doesn't return a City. It returns a *City — a pointer to a City. A memory address. And when you compare two pointers with ==, Go doesn't ask "do these point to the same value?" It asks "are these the exact same address in memory?" Alice and Bob are two separate Person structs living in two separate places in memory. Alice's city field lives at, say, address 0xc0000b4010. Bob's city field lives at 0xc0000b4030. Different houses. Different addresses. Even though both houses have "London" written on the door. The contents are identical. The addresses are not. And == on pointers only cares about addresses. The Fix Is Obvious Once You See The Bug If you want to compare values, return values: One * removed. Now alice.City() == bob.City() asks "is London equal to London?" and correctly answers true. Why Does This Pattern Exist At All? Fair question. Returning a pointer to a field isn't always wrong. There are legitimate reasons: Reason 1: You want the caller to be able to mutate the field. This is intentional mutability through a back-door. It's powerful. It's also a loaded gun pointed at your codebase's maintainability. Reason 2: You're working with large structs and want to avoid copies. If city were a massive struct (it isn't here), returning a pointer avoids copying it. Valid — but in practice, Go's compiler is smarter than most people give it credit for, and premature pointer optimization is a well-worn path to subtle bugs. Reason 3: You need to express "optional" / nullable. A *City can be nil. A City cannot. If the absence of a city is meaningful, a pointer communicates that. But *string and *int for nullable primitives should still make your eyes narrow — that's usually a job for a wrapper type or a dedicated Valid bool field. In Alice and Bob's case? None of these reasons apply. Returning &p.city here is a trap with no reward. The Smell Test Here's a rule of thumb worth keeping in your back pocket: If you're returning a pointer to a primitive, a string, or a simple value type — stop and ask why. Not "never do it." Just: why? What does the caller get from a *string that they wouldn't get from a string? If the answer isn't one of the three reasons above — mutability, avoiding large copies, or expressing nil — then you're probably handing someone a loaded footgun labeled "equality works normally here, trust me." The dangerous part isn't even the bug itself. The dangerous part is that it looks like it should work. alice.City() == bob.City() is perfectly valid Go. It compiles without complaint. The compiler isn't wrong — you can compare two *City values. It's just comparing the wrong thing. This is the category of bug where Go's type system can't save you, your tests might not catch it (because your test might use the same struct instance for both sides), and it sits quietly in production until someone notices that two users in the same city are being treated as if they're in different ones. One More Twist Here's where it gets truly devious. Consider this: Still false. Even though aliceCopy is a byte-for-byte copy of alice, it's a separate copy sitting at a different memory address. Their city fields are in different locations. And this: true! Because aliceRef.City() calls City() on the same underlying struct. Same struct, same field, same address. Pointers are about identity (where something lives), not equality (what it contains). Every time you see * in a return type, ask yourself which one the caller actually needs. The Moral Go doesn't hide what it's doing. *City in the return type is an honest signal: "I'm giving you an address, not a value." The language is telling you the truth. The trap is that we read code at a higher level of abstraction than the language executes it. We see alice.City() == bob.City() and our brain fills in "are they in the same city?" — a value comparison. But Go faithfully executes "are these two memory addresses identical?" — a pointer comparison. The code does exactly what it says. We just weren't reading carefully. So: return &field only when you mean it. Return values when you want value semantics. And when you see *string or *SomeSmallType in a return signature out in the wild, let your nose wrinkle — there's probably a story behind it, and it's rarely a happy one. If this saved you from a future production incident, share it with the Gopher in your life who deserves a heads up. 🐹

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/golang-secret-burned-me-2-hour-production-make-you-better-kumar-kkyae?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3B5i5r%2FTc4Tpqxoc358K0Rqg%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=1PqsiPiBwnvs81&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mlrlwdr5~qy-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mlrlwdr5-qy
  
One of Go's most misunderstood features I want to tell you about the day I stared at a timestamp bug for two hours. The logs made no sense. Two lines. Same function. The times were identical — even though one of them was supposed to fire 10 seconds later. I had sprinkled a defer in my code like a good little Gopher, expecting it to capture the world when it ran. But Go had other plans. That bug taught me something beautiful about how Go thinks. And once you see it, you cannot unsee it. The Code That Will Rewire Your Brain Quick — what does this print? Take a moment. Really think about it. ... Most engineers say: "The first timestamp, then 10 seconds later, the second timestamp." They are wrong. The actual output is two timestamps that are nearly identical — microseconds apart — even though the program takes 10 full seconds to finish. Why? The Rule That Changes Everything Here is the rule, and it is elegant in its simplicity: defer evaluates its arguments immediately. It only delays the call. Read that again. Slowly. When Go encounters defer fmt.Println(time.Now()), it does two things right then and there, before moving on to the next line: It evaluates time.Now() — captures the timestamp at that exact moment It says: "I'll call fmt.Println with this already-computed value when the function returns" The argument is frozen in time. It's like taking a photograph. The defer holds onto that photograph, not a live camera feed. So the timeline looks like this: The deferred Println runs at T+10, but it prints the value from T+0. The sleep is irrelevant to the value. It's already been decided. The Mental Model: Eager Arguments, Lazy Execution Think of defer as a reservation system. When you call defer f(x), Go immediately evaluates x, takes a note of the result, and books a reservation: "Call f with this exact value when the function exits." It's not saying: "At exit time, go figure out what x is." This distinction is everything. The value was locked in the moment defer was written. The future mutation of x is irrelevant. Where This Bites People (Real World Pain) The Logging Trap Wait — does this work? Let's think carefully. time.Since(start) is the argument to log.Printf. So it gets evaluated immediately, at the defer line, before any work is done. This would always log something like 127ns. This is a bug. The fix: By wrapping in an anonymous function, the entire function body is deferred — meaning time.Since(start) is now evaluated when the deferred func runs, not when it's declared. This is the idiomatic Go pattern for deferring logic that needs fresh values at exit time. The Loop Trap Here, each defer captures the value of i at the time of that iteration. This is actually correct behavior! Each iteration locks in its own value. The output is in reverse order (defers are LIFO — last in, first out), but each number is right. The Beautiful Duality of Defer There's a poetry to how defer works, once you understand it. It separates what from when. What to call, and with what arguments — decided now, at declaration time When to execute — decided later, at function exit This is a deliberate, thoughtful design choice. It means: You can reason about a defer's arguments locally, right where you wrote it, without needing to think about what values might look like at function exit. Resources are cleaned up with the context they were opened with. If you open a file and immediately defer file.Close(), the Close will always operate on that exact file handle, not some potentially-mutated version of a variable. Beautiful. Predictable. Safe. The Three Laws of Defer (Tattoo These On Your Brain) Law 1: Arguments are evaluated immediately. The value passed to a deferred function is computed at the defer statement, not at call time. Law 2: Deferred functions run LIFO. Last deferred = first to run. Like a stack. This is why cleanup code works elegantly: acquire A, acquire B, defer release B, defer release A. B is released before A. Perfect. Law 3: Deferred functions can read and modify named return values. This one is for another article, but know that a deferred function can affect what a function returns — if the return values are named. This is how some Go error wrapping patterns work. Why This Makes Go Special Languages with finally blocks (Java, Python, etc.) evaluate everything at execution time. You get fresh values, but the cleanup logic is separated from the resource acquisition — visually, conceptually, syntactically far away. Go's defer keeps cleanup right next to the thing being cleaned up: Two lines. Together. The relationship is obvious. The intent is clear. And because arguments are captured eagerly, you get a guarantee: the defer will always run with the values it saw at the moment of its declaration, unaffected by everything that happens afterward. That's not a quirk. That's a feature. That's Go being honest with you about what it promises to do. The Takeaway Next time you write defer, ask yourself: "Are any of these arguments something I want evaluated NOW versus at exit time?" If you want NOW: pass it directly. defer f(x) — x is captured immediately. If you want LATER: wrap it. defer func() { f(x) }() — x is evaluated when the deferred function runs. One mental model. Two clear patterns. Zero surprises. A Note of Appreciation I love Go for moments like this. The language has opinions. It makes choices that feel strange at first, then feel right once you understand the reasoning. Defer is not broken. Defer is not confusing once you know the rule. Defer is consistent — a quality more valuable in a programming language than almost anything else. Go isn't trying to protect you from yourself with magic. It's giving you a clear, inspectable mental model and trusting you to use it well. That's the Go philosophy. And that's why, after all these years, I still wake up excited to write it. If this rewired something in your brain, share it. Every Go engineer deserves to learn this before it bites them in production — not after. Happy coding. Keep reading the spec. 🐹

  Beware of Fake KYC Update Requests 
	

Fraudsters are posing as Bank officials 
to misuse your Banking Details 
	
	
	
	

	
	
	
	

Dear HDFC Bank Customer, 

Fraudsters are posing as bank officials via SMS, WhatsApp, or calls. 
They claim your account will be blocked unless RE-KYC is completed , and send a link to update your details. 

This link opens a fake app or site. Any information entered can be misused to access your Bank Account or make fraudulent transactions. 
Sharing such details can put your account at serious risk. 

Stay Alert! 
To protect yourself from Re-KYC fraud, follow these simple rules: 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Don’t act on unknown KYC update requests. Contact your Bank or visit a Branch to confirm. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Never download any app or file from suspicious or unverified sources. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

The Bank will never ask for your account details, passwords, or OTPs via call, SMS, or email. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

Report suspicious calls or messages on the Chakshu portal at  https://t13.mailers.hdfcbank.bank.in/r/?id=t972fcb3a-a24b-4074-b769-b7825ef36736,236a7c,a6564 sancharsaathi.gov.in  or via the Sanchar Saathi app. 
	
	
	
	

	
	

If you’ve fallen victim to such fraud, immediately contact your bank.

Go Memory Model · Bulb Moment
Channels don't just pass data — they pass time.
email_text:
Golang: The Random Chapters

By Abhishek Kumar


By Abhishek Kumar

    
    
    Read this article on LinkedIn to join the conversation
Read on LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/go-memory-model-bulb-moment-channels-dont-just-pass-data-kumar-ogcnc?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Bp6h%2BbyqDRYO1gkgqvYahQQ%3D%3D&midToken=AQEIM4HzHiyK2w&midSig=0LZUKARFPMuc81&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-ghmp60~mlqjvdgd~gp-null-null&eid=ghmp60-mlqjvdgd-gp
  
I used to think Go channels were just typed queues — a neat way to move values between goroutines. Then I stumbled onto the Go Memory Model's channel guarantees and had a full stop, re-read-it-twice moment. An unbuffered channel isn't just sending a value. It's creating a hard synchronization point — a moment where one goroutine can't move forward until the other shows up. That handshake also orders everything that happened before it. sync_demo.go 🔑 The rule: In an unbuffered channel, the nth receive happens-before the nth send completes — and vice versa. Both goroutines see all writes the other made before the handshake. The channel is a time contract, not just a pipe. This is why the panics are genuinely, provably impossible — not just unlikely. The Go Memory Model gives you an iron guarantee. You don't need mutexes here. The channel is the lock. Next time you reach for a out of habit — ask yourself: is there a channel handshake I could lean on instead?
